lesson.title: One Strand, Many Shapes: The Versatility of RNA
lesson.summary: RNA is a single stranded nucleic acid built from ribonucleotides that can fold back on itself, using the same complementary base pairing seen in DNA, to form a wide range of structured shapes that let it carry, decode, and even catalyze genetic information.
lesson.body:
RNA is built the same general way DNA is, a polymer of nucleotide monomers connected end to end by phosphodiester bonds into a sugar phosphate backbone. The nucleotide monomers are ribonucleotides rather than deoxyribonucleotides, meaning the sugar is ribose rather than deoxyribose, and the base uracil takes the place of thymine, pairing with adenine just as thymine would. Beyond that substitution, RNA still uses adenine, guanine, and cytosine as its other three bases, and it is still assembled through the same condensation chemistry described earlier for nucleic acids generally.

The most obvious structural difference from DNA is that RNA is normally single stranded rather than double stranded. That single strand is not locked into pairing with a separate, complementary strand the way DNA is, so it is free to fold back and pair with itself. Wherever one stretch of an RNA molecule happens to have a base sequence complementary to another stretch further along the same strand, adenine pairing with uracil and guanine pairing with cytosine, hydrogen bonds can form between them, and the RNA folds into short, local double helical regions, often shaped like hairpins or stem loops, even though it is still technically one continuous strand.

Different classes of RNA use this self-folding ability to very different degrees. Messenger RNA, or mRNA, stays comparatively unstructured along most of its length, since its main job is simply to carry a copy of a protein-coding sequence from DNA to the ribosome to be read. Transfer RNA, or tRNA, folds extensively into a cloverleaf pattern of stem loops that then packs further into a compact, L-shaped three-dimensional structure, with one end carrying a specific amino acid and another end, the anticodon loop, pairing transiently with the mRNA sequence being translated. Ribosomal RNA, or rRNA, folds into large, elaborate three-dimensional structures that form the physical core of the ribosome itself, and it is folded rRNA, not any protein, that directly catalyzes the formation of each new peptide bond during translation, the same peptide bond forming step introduced earlier.

Part of the reason RNA plays such a different structural role than DNA traces back to that single extra hydroxyl group on ribose's second carbon. That hydroxyl group makes the RNA backbone noticeably more chemically reactive, and more prone to hydrolysis, than the deoxyribose backbone of DNA, which is one reason RNA is generally less chemically stable over long timescales. This instability is part of why DNA, not RNA, typically serves as the long-term genetic archive in most organisms, although RNA does serve as the primary genetic material in certain viruses, including retroviruses and coronaviruses.

Because a single RNA molecule can both carry sequence information the way DNA does and fold into precise three-dimensional shapes that perform chemistry the way proteins do, RNA sits at an interesting midpoint between the two, which is part of why many scientists have proposed that an early stage of life on Earth may have relied primarily on RNA, an idea known as the RNA world hypothesis, before DNA and proteins took over their more specialized roles.
